relationships.title: Session of First Presbyterian Church North Port v. Presbytery of Southwest Florida

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.

Joined with Case 2009-25; the Session of Grace Presbyterian Church complained that views 3, 4, 5, and 6 in Northern California Presbytery's resolution on diaconal practice violated the BCO. The SJC sustained the complaint on the same grounds as 2009-25, annulling the abstract resolution while declining to rule on the constitutional merits of any specific diaconal view.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC addressed whether a presbytery and its administrative/judicial commission could suspend a local session and assume original jurisdiction over charges against a ruling elder. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot "act for" a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. The Presbytery's and Commission's actions, including the censure approved by Presbytery, were reversed.

metadata.synopsis: After Korean Capital Presbytery appointed a commission to suspend the functions of Korean Presbyterian Church Washington’s elected Session and replace them without prior congregational consent, TE Sung Keon Kim complained. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery violated Preliminary Principle Six and BCO 16-2, misread BCO 13-9, and impermissibly sought to act for the lower court. Relying on Chappell, it annulled the commission’s subsequent actions as the Session.

TE John P. Clark, Jr. appealed his conviction for contumacy and suspension/deposition by Southwest Presbytery's Judicial Commission. The SJC found the appeal in order (17-4) and remanded the case for retrial (21-0) on grounds that the Judicial Commission committed significant procedural errors, including abandoning original charges and convicting Clark of contumacy on new charges without giving him opportunity to respond.

The SJC affirmed Heartland Presbytery's judgment in all respects, with a concurring opinion finding three of four specifications invalid but deferring to the lower court's factfinding on the remaining specification.

metadata.synopsis: Smith complained that Northeast Presbytery failed to provide pastoral care after dissolving Grace Presbyterian Church. The SJC rejected Presbytery's objections that the complaint lacked supporting reasons or was barred by Smith's protest, held it in order, but denied it on the merits. Distinguishing the pastoral 'power of order' from judicial 'power of jurisdiction,' the SJC ruled that the Constitution neither requires nor permits a presbytery to retain jurisdiction over individual members of a dissolved particular church, and that pastoral care of former members is generally discretionary; on these facts, Presbytery's efforts satisfied any duty.

metadata.synopsis: A complaint arising from Central Carolina Presbytery’s refusal to prosecute TE Stephen O. Stout and to recognize his accusers as voluntary prosecutors was denied. The SJC framed two issues and answered both yes: the Presbytery could constitutionally adopt its Investigative Committee report and decline judicial process, because the Committee found no “strong presumption of guilt” under BCO 31-2; and it could refuse voluntary-prosecutor status, because BCO 31-1/31-3 left discipline to the Presbytery and made any voluntary prosecutor subject to its approval. The complaint was denied on both issues.

metadata.synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

topics: fundamentals of the system of doctrine
suspension from office without due process
metadata.synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

topics: suspension of session without due process
metadata.synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

metadata.synopsis: Teaching Elder Wallace Marshall complained against the same Eastern Carolina Presbytery actions at Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church that were the subject of Case 90-4, filed separately as a Teaching Elder complainant. The SJC sustained this complaint on essentially the same grounds as Case 90-4, finding that the presbytery lacked authority to suspend the session without due process and to constitute itself as a 'Session Pro Tem.'
